en: The Kośāmbaka-vastu (MSV II 173). In the Kośāmbaka-vastu, there is this summary verse (uddāna):
The quarrel of the Kośāmbakas and their discord with the monks;
the dispute over the recitation and the journey of Dīrghika.
Bhṛgu was protected in the salt-house by a wild elephant,
and having thus [rescued] Aniruddha as well, he attained peace in Śrāvastī.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kośāmbī in the Ghoṣila Monastery.
At that time, there was a monk from Kośāmbī who was fierce and courageous, a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās;
he had many fellow monks as his companions, all of whom were likewise fierce and courageous, masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkās.
In Vaiśālī there was a monk from Vaiśālī who was fierce and courageous, a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās;
he had many fellow monks who were likewise fierce and courageous, masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkās.
Then, on another occasion, that monk from Vaiśālī, while wandering on a tour through the countryside, arrived at Kośāmbī.
Having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he approached the monk Kośāmbaka.
Having approached him and exchanged greetings with one another, they began to reach a definitive conclusion regarding the teachings of the Sūtras and Vinaya.
Then, one of them said:
"This sūtra should be recited in this way.
This is the meaning of this sūtra. A second person says: "This sūtra should not be recited in this way."
This is not the meaning of this sūtra:
"What is improper for you is proper for me; what is consistent for you [is inconsistent for me]."
"It is not for me;
it is for you.
Thereupon, mutual hostility arose between the two of them.
The monk from Kośāmbī remained intent on seeking out the faults of the one from Vaiśālī;
however, the Saṅgha has made this formal agreement:
"Whoever sees that the chamber-pot is empty, hollow, and devoid of water, shall fill it with water and place it back in its proper position, or inform the steward of the requisites."
"The chamber-pot for excrement stands empty.

If one does not fill it oneself, nor inform the attendant in charge of the requisites, one is guilty of negligence. And because of that negligence, we shall cause him to confess an offense involving expiation (pāyantika).
At one time, a certain householder invited the community of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a meal at his home. There, some of the monks had already gone to eat,
while others were about to go.
A monk from Vaiśālī, having taken his chamber-pot, entered the latrine.
His co-resident, moving with hurried steps, went to call him, saying:
"Preceptor, some monks have gone to eat, while others are about to go."
"Come, let us go. Having set down the chamber-pot with him in one place, he set out.
And that monk from Kośāmbī arrived at that spot.
Then that monk from Vaiśālī, taking his chamber-pot in hand, began to enter the monastery. His co-resident said to him,
"Preceptor, why do you enter again?"
He said,
"Son, this monk from Kośāmbī is looking for an opportunity against me;
I am entering only to fill my chamber-pot."
"Is this entirely empty in every respect?
"Not entirely in every respect;
however, it is not possible to perform the function of water with this water."
"Preceptor, may you alone be entirely empty of everything!
We are the Preceptor’s faction, his strength, and his allies.
Come!"
"Let us go.
He left her right there and went with him.
She was seen by the monk from Kośāmbī, and that water-jar was seized by him.
Then, overcome with indignation, he uttered "Hum," filled his water-pot, attended to his bodily needs, and departed. Later,
when the community of monks had finished their meal and returned to the monastery, he began to distribute [the food] among the monks.

"Venerable ones, this monk from Vaiśālī has broken the formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) of the Saṃgha. Then, performing the proper salutation according to seniority, he approached him in due order and said:
"Venerable one, grant me the opportunity.
"It is granted. "He has fallen into an offense."
"Act according to the Dharma;
I do not see any offense.

Has it not been established by the Saṃgha as a formal agreement that whoever sees the chamber-pot empty, hollow, and waterless must fill it with water himself and place it back in its proper position?"
Or it should be reported to the steward: "Venerable sir, the chamber-pot is empty. If he does not fill it himself, [the steward should do so].
Nor does he inform the superintendent; he shows him disrespect. And because of that disrespect, we shall cause him to confess a *pāyantika* offense.
He said,
"It is not empty;
let it not be empty."
It was not possible for him to perform any purpose with that water;
he remained silent.
That monk from Kośāmbī was a resident of Kośāmbī and had a large retinue.
Because he had performed an act of suspension against him by force, the monks of Vaiśālī became agitated.
Thereupon, a quarrel, a dispute, a conflict, and a contention arose between the monks of Kośāmbī and those of Vaiśālī, namely: "Is he guilty of an offense? or "Is he not guilty of an offense?"
Furthermore, one who has fallen [into an offense] is not one who has not fallen;
one who has been suspended is not one who has not been suspended.
Moreover, one who has been suspended is so by means of an illegal action—one that is contested and subject to suspension.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One summoned by messenger the suspended monk, the monk who sided with the suspended one, and those who sided with the one who sided with the suspended one, and said this to them:
"Is it true, monks, that a quarrel, a dispute, a contention, and a conflict have arisen among you—namely, 'one is guilty' and so forth, as before, up to 'one is censurable and fit for suspension'?"
"It is true, Venerable Sir.
Monks, let there be no quarreling, no strife, no contention, and no dispute.
Rather, I shall prescribe the rules of conduct for a monk who has been suspended."
A monk who has been subject to the *utkṣepaka* (suspension) procedure should produce this thought:
"This monk who suspended me is fierce and powerful; he is a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās.
Moreover, he has many monks as his companions, who are also fierce and powerful, masters of the Sūtras, masters of the Vinaya, and masters of the Mātṛkās."
"If I do not rectify my offense according to the Dharma,
because of that the Saṃgha will dwell embroiled in strife, embroiled in quarrels, contentious, and fallen into dispute.
What if I were to rectify my offense according to the Dharma?"
If a monk who has been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*) does not undertake and abide by the rules of proper conduct as they have been prescribed,
he becomes guilty of an offense.

Then the Blessed One [addressed] the suspended monk, the monks who side with the suspended monk (*utkṣiptakānuvartaka*), and the monks who side with those who side with the suspended monk (*utkṣiptakānuvartakānuvartaka*).
Having incited the monk who was the instigator, the monks who were followers of the instigator, and the monks who were followers of those followers,
he summoned them by messenger and said this:
"Is it true, monks, that a quarrel, a dispute, a contention, and a conflict have arisen among you— namely, 'one is guilty' or [the rest as before] up to 'one is fit for suspension'?"
"It is true, Venerable Sir.
Monks, let there be no quarreling, no strife, no contention, and no dispute.
Nevertheless, I shall prescribe the rules of conduct for a monk who has performed an act of suspension."
The monk who performs the formal act of suspension should arouse this thought:
"This suspended monk is fierce, courageous, a master of the Sūtras, a master of the Vinaya, and a master of the Mātṛkās."
"He has many fellow monks as his companions—men who are fierce, courageous, and experts in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās.
If I were to urge him or remind him against his will, the Saṃgha would live embroiled in quarrels, strife, contention, and disputes.
What if I were not to urge him or remind him against his will?"
A monk who has been subject to the *utkṣepaka* (suspension) offense incurs a transgression if he does not undertake and abide by the rules of conduct as they have been prescribed.
Even though they were addressed in this way by the Blessed One, those monks continued to dwell having fallen into quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute.
Now, even on the day of the *poṣadha*, they were observing it as a non-*poṣadha* day.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having summoned by messenger the suspended monk, the monks who followed the suspended one, and the monks who followed those who followed the suspended one, said this to them:
"Is it true, monks, that even though you are addressed by me in this way, you continue to dwell engaged in quarreling, brawling, disputing, and falling into contention?
Do you even now, on the day of the Poṣadha, wait for a non-Poṣadha?
"It is true, Venerable Sir."
"Monks, let there be no quarreling, no strife, no contention, and no dispute.

For you who dwell having given rise to quarreling, monks, having given rise to strife, being contentious, and having fallen into dispute— whatever formal acts (*karma*) are performed, such as the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, a motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñaptidvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha*)— "
Regarding the action: actions that have been performed become subject to censure.
O monks, you are those who dwell apart from those monks, and they are those who dwell apart from you.
For what reason?
Monks, there are these two who belong to different residences (*nānāsaṃvāsika*):
one who establishes himself as belonging to a different residence, and [the other].
Or, one who is established by the Saṃgha according to the Dharma—
how can he himself establish himself as one living apart?
It is, for example, when monks who are quarreling, disputing, contending, and fallen into conflict with one another, remaining divided into factions and counter-factions, intentionally [act].

When one moves from the side of the Dharma to the side of non-Dharma, in this way one establishes oneself as one who is of separate residence by one's own self. How is one established [as such] by the Saṃgha?
Just as, for instance, one is suspended by the Saṃgha itself for not seeing [one's offense],
or is suspended for not making amends, or for not relinquishing an evil view—
so too is it done by the Saṃgha according to the Dharma.
Monks, there are these two who are members of the same community.
Which two?
He who establishes himself as being of the same community by his own accord, and [he who is so established by another].
Or, one who is established by the Saṃgha according to the Dharma—
how does he establish himself as one living in communion by himself?
It is, for example, when monks are dwelling in a state of quarreling, brawling, and being at odds with other monks.
When those who have fallen into dispute are established in opposing factions, he intentionally causes them to transfer from the faction of non-Dharma to the faction of Dharma.
In this way, by himself, he establishes himself as one who shares the same communal residence. How, then, is he established by the Saṃgha according to the Dharma?
Just as one who has been suspended by the Saṃgha for not seeing [an offense] is reinstated;
or one who has been suspended for not making amends or for not relinquishing an evil view is reinstated—
in this same way, the Saṃgha acts according to the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the suspended monk, the monks who sided with the suspended monk, and the monks who sided with those who sided with the suspended monk, sent a messenger to summon the suspending monk, the monks who sided with the suspending monk, and the monks who sided with those who sided with the suspending monk,
and said this to them: "Is it true, monks, that even though you have been addressed by me in this way, you continue to dwell engaged in quarreling, wrangling, disputing, and contention?"
"Even now, on the day of the Poṣadha, you have arrived on a non-Poṣadha day?
"It is true, Venerable Sir."

As before, even though they were addressed by the Blessed One in this way, those monks continued to dwell in a state of quarreling, brawling, contending, and falling into disputes. Then, a certain householder invited the Saṅgha of monks, headed by the Buddha, to a meal at his home,
and the Saṅgha of monks entered.
The Blessed One remained in the possession of material goods, having accepted almsfood.

For five reasons, the Buddha-Blessed Ones remain in the possession of material goods, having accepted almsfood, as previously described, up until: in this matter, the Blessed One, desiring to prescribe a rule of training for his disciples regarding the Vinaya, remained in the possession of material goods, having accepted almsfood.

And there, while the monks who were both plaintiffs and defendants had entered a house to eat, a quarrel, a scuffle, a conflict, and a dispute arose among them— namely, "one is guilty," and so on as before,
up to "one is liable for formal suspension"—
and they even went so far as to strike one another.
Then the monk who had brought the alms-food, taking the alms-food, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and placed the alms-food to one side, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood before him.
It is indeed the nature of things that the Buddha-Blessed Ones greet the monk who has brought the alms-food with this greeting:
"Is the food excellent, monk? Has the community of monks been satisfied?
Thus did the Blessed One greet the monk who had brought the alms-food with this greeting:
"Is the food excellent, monk? Has the community of monks been satisfied?"
"It is true, venerable sir;
the excellent food has satisfied the community of monks.
However, a quarrel and dispute has arisen among the monks who were litigants and adversaries within the house."
The dispute was a quarrel, namely that [the monk] was "one who has fallen" (*āpanna*), as previously described, up to the point of being fit for formal censure (*sthāpanārha*).
Furthermore, they even came to blows with one another.
Then the Blessed One, having finished his meal, washed his feet outside the monastery and entered the monastery for seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*).
Then the Blessed One, having arisen from his seclusion in the evening, sat down on the seat prepared for him in front of the community of monks.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Is it true, monks, that while you were entering a house to eat, there arose among you quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute—namely, 'Has he committed an offense? or as before, up to: 'Even now...'"?
They have even come to mutual blows.
Truly so, Venerable Sir.
Monks, let there be no quarreling, no strife, no contention, and no dispute.
Furthermore, I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for monks who have entered the homes of litigants and their opponents.
When monks who are litigants or opponents have entered a home, they should sit screened from one another by their seats, so that there is no opportunity for such improper physical behavior to occur.
When monks who are litigants enter a house, if they do not undertake and abide by the customary rules as they have been prescribed,
they become guilty of an offense.
Even when addressed in this way by the Blessed One, those monks continued to dwell having fallen into quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, let there be no quarreling, no brawling, no strife, and no dispute."

"O monks, it is impossible that you, while living in a state of quarreling, brawling, contending, and falling into disputes, will subdue and pacify each successive legal issue according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction.
However, O monks, it is possible that you, while living without quarreling, without brawling, without contending, and without falling into disputes..."

"Whenever legal disputes arise, you shall subdue them, pacify them, and bring them to complete cessation through the Dharma, through the Vinaya, and through the Teacher’s instruction; this is possible.
Long ago, monks, there were two kings, Brahmadatta, the king of Kāśi, and Dīrghila, the king of Kosala, who were at enmity with one another."
The *Dīrghila-sūtra* is found in detail in the *Samādhi-saṃyukta* section of the *Madhyama-āgama*.
They say this, and furthermore,
the Blessed One has spoken thus:
Suffering is King Brahmadatta and the exhaustion of enjoyments;
suffering is death in a foreign land and the failure to see one's kinsmen.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Let those who speak discordantly and move with equal speed not think, 'This is not the best.
For when the Saṅgha is being split, let no one consider even a small matter as insignificant."
For those who pierce the bones of living beings, those who seize the cattle, horses, and wealth of others,
and those who plunder the kingdom—
why would there not be a reunion for you, who understand this Dharma?
Those who appear to be wise, yet grasp at the sphere of speech and speak of it, are led astray by that perverse [ignorance] from the mouths of those striving [in vain]; thus they do not know.
Others here do not understand: "We are striving for this. But for those who do understand, their quarrels are stilled.
"He reviled me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—
for those who harbor such thoughts, their enmity is never stilled.
"Those who do not harbor enmity toward those who have reviled me, spoken against me, defeated me, or caused me to lose what was mine— their enmity is stilled."
For enmities are never appeased in this world by enmity;
enmities are appeased through patience—this is the eternal law.
For enmity is never appeased by enmity; enmities are pacified by the absence of enmity.
Indeed, the pursuit of enmity leads to harm for embodied beings; therefore, the wise person does not harbor enmity.
If one should find a prudent companion, a fellow traveler who is steadfast in virtuous conduct, one should dwell with him,
having overcome all outflows, joyful and mindful.
If one does not find a prudent companion to walk with, a steadfast fellow-practitioner, one should wander alone like a king who has renounced a vast kingdom; let him not commit evil deeds.
If, while wandering, one does not find a superior who is equal to oneself, one should maintain a firm solitary practice; for there is no companionship with a fool.
The conduct of one alone is better than companionship with fools;
one should wander alone with little concern, like an elephant in a forest of Mātaṅgas.
When this had been said, the monks of Kośāmbī said this to the Blessed One:
"The Blessed One is the Lord of Dharma; the Sugata is the Lord of Dharma."
"These people will speak ill of us, uttering harsh words and insults;
why should we tolerate them?
Then the Blessed One was displeased and dissatisfied with those monks because of their manner, their conduct, and their misconduct.
Then, by means of that very supernatural power, he departed through the air above and set out on a journey toward Śrāvastī; traveling by stages,
he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed there in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
When the Blessed One had departed from there, such was the conduct of the monks of Kośāmbī and the monks of Vaiśālī:
they entered for alms even before the morning meal, and after the midday meal, having bolted the doors, they engaged in quarreling.
Thus, through that manner of conduct, behavior, and transgression, twelve years passed for them.
The brahmins and householders of Kośāmbī began to converse with one another in the assembly hall:
"Sirs, we are exceedingly devoted to the Blessed One, providing him with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
yet, despite this domain having been abandoned by the Blessed One for twelve years, he does not come even until today."

Others said, "Sirs, the Blessed One will come here, for now these monks of Kośāmbī exhibit such behavior, conduct, and misconduct: they enter for alms before the morning meal, and after the midday meal, having bolted the door, they engage in quarreling."
But others said:
"Sirs, this fault does not belong to them; rather, it belongs to us, we who provide them with alms-food or engage in conversation with them.
We shall establish this formal agreement."

"No one shall give them almsfood, nor shall they even engage them in conversation. Having made this formal agreement, they remained established in it. Then, on another day, the monks of Kośāmbī entered for alms.

No one spoke to them, nor was any alms-food offered. Just as they had entered for alms with their bowls washed, so did they depart with their bowls washed. Having failed to obtain even a single morsel of food, they gathered together and spoke to the brahmins and householders of Kośāmbī.
"Sirs, it is first of all improper that you do not offer us almsfood, saying that our resources are exhausted;
what offense have we committed that you will not even grant us a word?"
They said,
"You also claim for yourselves, 'We are śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya,' yet your teacher is displeased and dissatisfied with your deportment, conduct, and misconduct."
He departed through the air above;
twelve years have passed, yet even today he does not return.
They remained there in silence.
Having approached them, they said:
"Venerable ones, we have been brought to ruin by these men;
he who stumbles upon the earth must rely on those very feet to rise again."
"In every way we shall go to Śrāvastī;
we shall ask forgiveness from the Blessed One and the community of monks.
Then, at the end of that very night, the monks of Kośāmbī took up their bowls and robes and, without even entering Kośāmbī, set out on a wandering tour toward Śrāvastī.

The venerable Ānanda heard that the monks of Kośāmbī were coming—those who create strife, quarrels, disputes, and legal issues; those by whom the Blessed One was insulted when he came here. "They will reproach us and remind us with shamelessness or with harshness," he thought. "What if I were to inform the Blessed One? Having understood this, he went to where the Blessed One was.
He approached him;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I have heard that the monks of Kośāmbī are coming here—those who create strife, quarrels, disputes, and contention, and who are litigants;
those by whom the Blessed One was insulted when he came here. They will reproach us and remind us, whether out of shamelessness or out of malice."
"How should we behave toward them?
"Ānanda, monks should not speak to them, nor converse with them, nor look at them, nor gaze at them; they should assign them peripheral lodgings except by means of hand gestures.
If they say, 'We are elders; why are peripheral lodgings assigned to us?'"
They should be told:

"You yourselves claim to be śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya; yet your teacher, being displeased and dissatisfied with your deportment, conduct, and misconduct, has come here by means of his supernatural power—our compassionate teacher—who has authorized this very act."
"Even this has not occurred to you.

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī heard that the monks of Kośāmbī were coming— those who create strife, those who create quarrels, those who create disputes, those who create contention, and those who bring about legal cases— and having heard this, she thought to herself:
"I am going; I shall see the Blessed One. Having understood how she should conduct herself toward them, she approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, I have heard that the monks of Kośāmbī are coming—those who create quarrels, those who create strife, those who cause discord, those who cause disputes, and those who bring about legal cases. How should I conduct myself toward them?
You, Gautamī, must not converse with the monks of Kośāmbī, nor speak with them, nor look at them, nor gaze upon them; rather, as soon as you see them, you should simply take your seat."

Thinking, "This is the senior assembly," the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the monks from Kośāmbī were arriving— those who create strife, those who create quarrels, those who create disputes, those who create contention, and those who bring about legal cases. Upon hearing this, the following thought occurred to him:
Thinking, "I shall go and see the Blessed One; how should I conduct myself toward them? and having understood this, he approached the place where the Blessed One was.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada said this to the Blessed One:

"Venerable sir, I have heard that the monks of Kośāmbī are coming—those who create quarrels, those who create strife, those who create disputes, those who create contention, and those who cause legal issues. How should I conduct myself toward them? "Householder, you should not converse with the monks of Kośāmbī."
"They should not converse with them, nor look at them, nor gaze at them, nor pay them homage; however, almsfood may be given, for giving does not conflict [with the rule].
Thus instructed, the Kośāmbaka monks gradually arrived at Śrāvastī.
There, having set aside their bowls and robes and washed their feet, they asked,
"Who is the assigner of lodgings? The attendants replied.
"Noble Ānanda! they said, and they approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached, they spoke thus to the Venerable Ānanda.
"Venerable Ānanda, assign us our lodgings. Venerable Ānanda began to assign them their most peripheral lodgings by means of manual gestures.
They said:
"Venerable Ānanda, we are old;
why are the lodgings in the border regions assigned to us?
He replied:
"You too are śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas," [he said], as before, up until: "even this does not apply to you.
They became distressed and passed the night with great difficulty.
Then, at the break of dawn, as the monk who had been suspended (utkṣiptaka) was reflecting upon his own mental continuum, this thought occurred to him:

Whatever quarrel, strife, dispute, or contention has arisen among us— namely, whether one has committed an offense or not, or whether one has been suspended from the community or not— I am indeed one who has committed an offense and not one who has not;
I am one who has been suspended and not one who has not.

Furthermore, having realized, "Since I have been suspended by means of a formal act that is legal, irreversible, and not subject to reinstatement, what if I were to effect a reconciliation and restore harmony? he rose early at dawn and went to where the monks who side with the suspended one and those who side with those who side with the suspended one were staying.
Having approached them, he spoke thus to the monks who side with the suspended one and to those who side with those who side with the suspended one:
"Venerable ones, as I was surveying my own mental continuum here at the break of dawn, this thought occurred to me:

'On account of what cause has there arisen for me this quarrel, strife, contention, and dispute— namely, whether one is "guilty of an offense" or "not guilty of an offense," or "suspended" or "not suspended"?'"
Thus, I am one who has been suspended,
not one who has not been suspended;
I have been suspended by means of a formal act that is in accordance with the Dharma, which is unshakeable and not subject to being set aside.
"I shall bring about a reconciliation; I shall create harmony. "What do you say?
They replied:
"So be it; well said.
Then the suspended monk, the monks who side with the suspended monk, and the monks who side with those who side with the suspended monk—
And he approached the monk who had been suspended, the monks who were followers of the one suspended, and the monks who were followers of those followers;
having approached them, he spoke thus to the suspended monk, the followers of the suspended monk, and the followers of those followers.
"Venerable sirs, as I was reflecting upon my own mental continuum here at the break of dawn this night, this thought occurred to me:
'On account of what cause did this quarrel and dispute arise for me—as described previously—up until the point where I might effect a reconciliation and restore harmony?
What will you do?"
They said,
"So be it; this is excellent."
That suspended monk, the monks who sided with the suspended one, the monks who sided with those who sided with the suspended one,
the suspending monk, the monks who sided with the suspender, and the monks who sided with those who sided with the suspender,
approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the monk Utkṣepaka said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, as I was examining my own mental continuum here at the time of dawn, this thought occurred to me:"
"I shall bring about the prior connection;
that is, I shall mobilize all these monks toward harmony.
The Blessed One said: [Thus it was].

"Excellent, excellent, monk! One who brings about reconciliation and harmony among monks who are living in strife, engaged in quarrels, contentious, fallen into dispute, and divided into factions and counter-factions, produces much merit— immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless."
For just as if someone were to join together hair that had been cut into hundreds of pieces, knot by knot,

even so one generates immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless merit— whoever reconciles and brings about harmony among monks who have fallen into quarreling and are living [in discord], as previously described.
Furthermore, I shall prescribe the rules of conduct for a suspended monk (*utkṣiptaka*).
A suspended monk must request reinstatement from the Saṃgha.
And it should be requested in this manner:

Having prepared the bedding and seating, struck the gong, and questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṅgha has sat down and assembled, one should perform the proper salutation with respect according to seniority, sit crouching at the end of the elders, join the palms, and speak as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen.

On account of which cause there has arisen for me quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute— namely, whether one is 'guilty' or 'not guilty,' or 'suspended' or 'not suspended'— I am indeed guilty and not innocent, and I am suspended and not unsuspended."

Furthermore, I, the monk named [so-and-so], who have been suspended by a formal act (*karman*) that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to being set aside, hereby request reinstatement from the Saṃgha. May the venerable Saṃgha reinstate me.
"I shall act in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya,
out of compassion and taking compassion as my motive. Thus he says a second and a third time.
Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
For whatever reason, venerable sirs, there has arisen strife, quarreling, contention, and dispute—namely, the charge that 'one has fallen into an offense'."
Whether he is one who has not committed [an offense],
or one who has been suspended, or one who has not been suspended.
Thus, he is one who has fallen [into an offense], not one who has not fallen;
he is one who has been suspended, not one who has not been suspended—
provided that he was suspended by means of a formal act (*karman*) that is in accordance with the Dharma, irreversible, and not subject to being set aside.
This monk named so-and-so, having been suspended, requests reinstatement from the Saṃgha.
If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, if it approves, grant that the Saṃgha reinstate the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (karman) should be performed:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen! On account of which cause there has arisen among the Venerable Ones quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, as previously described, up to..."

This monk, named so-and-so, requests reinstatement from the Saṃgha. Therefore, the Saṃgha reinstates the monk named so-and-so. Those venerable ones who approve of the Saṃgha reinstating the monk named so-and-so, let them remain silent; those who do not approve, let them speak. Thus the Saṃgha reinstates the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
The formal act is to be performed:
May the venerable Saṃgha listen.
For this reason, Venerable Ones, a quarrel, a dispute, a contention, and a conflict have arisen, as previously described, up until this point.
This monk named so-and-so, having been suspended, now requests reinstatement from the Saṃgha.
Therefore, the Saṃgha reinstates the monk named so-and-so.
Those venerable ones who approve of reinstating the suspended monk named so-and-so should remain silent;
those who do not approve should speak.
"Let them speak:
'The monk named so-and-so, who had been suspended, has been reinstated by the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha has consented and authorized this."
Since you remain silent, I thus hold it so:
this is a formal act of reinstatement (osāraṇīya-karman). I shall now prescribe for that monk the duties of proper conduct (āsamudācārika-dharma).
A monk who has been subjected to the formal act of reinstatement (osāraṇīyakarma) must request harmony from the Saṃgha.
Furthermore, it should be requested in this manner:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen."
On account of which cause this quarrel, contention, strife, and dispute arose for me— namely, whether one has committed an offense or not,
or whether one has been suspended or not— I am indeed one who has committed an offense, and not one who has not.
One who has been suspended is not one who has not been suspended;
furthermore, he has been suspended by means of a formal act that is in accordance with the Dharma, which is irreversible and not subject to being set aside.
By me, [named] so-and-so...
The monk who has been subjected to the *utkṣepaka* (suspension) has requested reinstatement from the Saṃgha:
"The Saṃgha has performed for me the formal act of reinstatement (*osāraṇīya-karman*).
I, named so-and-so, having had the act of reinstatement performed upon me, request the Saṃgha of monks for their assembly."
"May the venerable Saṃgha grant the restoration of harmony to me, the monk named so-and-so who has been reinstated, out of compassion, taking compassion upon us. Thus a second time as well.
Thus it should be done three times.
Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen."
This is the cause for which this Venerable One has given rise to quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute—namely, [the charge] that he is "guilty," and so forth, as previously stated.

If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha consent and authorize that the Saṃgha grant the restoration of the formal act (*sāmagrī*) to the monk named so-and-so who has performed the act of reinstatement (*osāraṇīyakarma*).
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (*karma*) is to be performed:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen.

For whatever reason this dispute, quarrel, contention, and strife has arisen for this venerable one—namely, that he was previously accused [as stated above]—the Saṃgha has thus performed the formal act of reinstatement for the one named so-and-so."
The assembly of monks is in harmony;
it is accepted and approved.
Since there is silence, I shall hold it to be thus.
Thus, the formal assembly (sāmagrī) has been granted by the Saṃgha to this monk for whom the act of reinstatement (osāraṇīyakarman) has been performed;
the Saṃgha must grant him that assembly.
No remorse should be felt in this matter.
I shall prescribe the rules of proper conduct for a monk who has been granted by the harmony of the Saṃgha.
A monk who has been granted by the harmony of the Saṃgha must request the Poṣadha ceremony;
furthermore, it should be requested in this manner:
Having prepared the bedding and seats as before, up until:
"I, who am named so-and-so, being one to whom the Saṃgha has granted the status of a *sāmagrīdattaka*, request from the Saṃgha the *sāmagrī-poṣadha*.
May the venerable Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* to me, the monk named so-and-so, who am a *sāmagrīdattaka*."
Thus a second time, and a third time;
thereafter, one monk should make a formal motion (*jñapti*) and perform the ritual act (*karman*).

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. On account of which cause this dispute, quarrel, contention, and strife has arisen for this venerable one— namely, [the charge] that he is guilty, or as before, up to [the point where it is said]— this person of such-and-such a name, who has been granted the restoration of harmony by the Saṃgha, requests from the Saṃgha the Poṣadha ceremony of communal harmony."
If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha consent and authorize that the Saṃgha shall grant the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* to the monk named so-and-so, who has been granted the *saṃghasāmagrī*.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal act (*karman*) should now be performed.

Let the venerable Saṃgha listen. On account of which cause this dispute, quarrel, contention, and strife has arisen for this venerable one— namely, whether he is "guilty" or "not guilty," and so on as before— this one named so-and-so, who has been granted the restoration of harmony, requests from the Saṃgha the Poṣadha of communal harmony.
Therefore, the Saṃgha grants the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* to the monk named so-and-so, who has been granted the *sāmagrī*.
Those who consent to granting the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* to the monk named so-and-so, who has been granted the *sāmagrī*, should remain silent.
[It being so,] they are silent.
They do not consent.
Let them speak.
The Sangha has granted the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* to the monk named so-and-so, who is a recipient of the *sāmagrī-dattaka*.
The Saṃgha has consented and authorized this;
since there is silence, I shall hold it thus.
With whichever monk the Saṃgha has granted the *sāmagrī-poṣadha* (the communal confession), one should [perform it] together with him.

The Saṃgha should perform the Poṣadha while some members are seated, as well as the Pravāraṇā, the *jñapti*, the *jñapti-dvitīya*, and the *jñapti-caturtha* formal acts (*karman*). No remorse should be felt in this matter; those who perform them while discordant incur an offense of transgression.
Furthermore, a monk must not wait for the Poṣadha on a day that is not the Poṣadha;
he commits an offense,
except in the case of an auspicious Poṣadha or a Poṣadha for the sake of communal harmony.
The Kośāmbaka-vastu is completed.
